div.p: In a recent survey, it was observed that the majority of the respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in considered systems answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". Cyclic executives, though hardly addressed in contemporary text books, if at all, are therefore still in use in practice. Hence, there is a need for analysis techniques for these executives.

In earlier work, exact analysis for single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives, scheduling a given sequence of independent hard real-time polling tasks in single-processor systems, has been presented. Unlike the analysis for single-rate AFAP cyclic executives, the analysis for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives depends on the order of the tasks in the cycle. In this paper, we present a conjecture for an optimal order assignment (OOA) algorithm for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: As described in [1], cyclic executives are generally used in defense military systems and traffic control systems to handle periodic tasks. Cyclic executives effectively execute hard realtime tasks in a continuous loop, in which every task appears at least once. Since the paper by C. Douglass Locke [2], in which it is concluded that the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach for hard real-time systems, the academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased 1 . Accordingly, cyclic executives are mentioned in contemporary text books, such as [1], [4]- [6], but hardly addressed in detail. Despite the decreasing academic interest, cyclic executives are still in use, however. In a recent survey of 120 industry practitioners in the field of real-time embedded systems [7], it was observed that from the 97 respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". Availability of exact analysis for cyclic executives therefore remains desirable.

Earlier work [8] presented exact analysis for single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives and discussed their relative strength and weaknesses in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, and schedulability. These two cyclic executives turned out to be incompa-rable. On the one hand, a time-driven AFAP cyclic executive outperforms an AFAP cyclic executive when jitter and energy efficiency are considered. On the other hand, the AFAP cyclic executive dominates the time-driven AFAP cyclic executive from a schedulability perspective.

Whereas the worst-case analysis for single-rate AFAP cyclic executives is independent of the order of the tasks in the cycle, the worst-case analysis for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives is not. In this document, we therefore present a conjecture for an optimal order assignment (OOA) algorithm for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives.

The remainder of this document is organized as follows. In Section II, we present a basic real-time system model. In Section III, we provide a recap of the two basic single-rate cyclic executives considered, including their exact analysis. The OOA Algorithm is the topic of Section IV. We briefly discuss an option for further enhancement of our OOA algorithm in Section V and subsequently conclude the document in Section VI.

div.head: II. A BASIC REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume a system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Each event e i is characterized by a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple < e i , r i > is characterized by a best-case system deadline BD S i and a worstcase system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a best-case computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: We assume that tasks are scheduled by cyclic executives, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. The sequence of tasks executed in a cycle is assumed to be known statically. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization. When a system S meets all its deadlines under a specific cyclic executive and a specific sequence of tasks, the system S is called schedulable under that cyclic executive and that sequence.
For ease of presentation and without loss of generality, the jobs of tasks in a cycle are assumed to be executed in the order of increasing index.

div.head: III. RECAP OF CYCLIC EXECUTIVES AND THEIR ANALYSIS
div.p: For (basic) cyclic executives, tasks can simply be implemented as procedures and executed within a loop. A singlerate cyclic executive essentially executes every task exactly once in a cycle.

div.head: C. Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate time-driven AFAP, a cycle is started by a timer. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be less than the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e. 1≤i≤n WC i ≤ T S .

Figure 1 illustrates a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where the cycle is started at time Φ. By starting cycles with an inter-arrival time of T S , the spare time, i.e. the combination of slack time 2 and gain time 3 , can be used to execute background tasks or run the processor at a lower, more energy efficient, clock frequency after the cycle is completed.

div.head: IV. AN OPTIMAL ORDER ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHM
div.p: The worst-case schedulability analysis for the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive is dependent on the order of the tasks in the cycle; see (4). As an example, system S I is schedulable for a task order {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 }.

In this section, we first rewrite Theorem 2 to support an arbitrary, but fixed, order of tasks in a cycle. Next, we show that our example system S I is schedulable for task order {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 }. We subsequently provide a conjecture for an optimal task order assignment algorithm, and conclude with a proof sketch.

div.head: C. A conjecture and an OOA algorithm
div.p: We define an optimal order assignment (OOA) policy O for a set T S of tasks of a system S scheduled by means of a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive as an order assignment that will make S schedulable, iff such an order exists.

Conjecture 1. Given a system S and a set of tasks T S , the OOA algorithm (Algorithm 1) determines a sequence task[] that contains every task of T S exactly once, for which S is schedulable under a single-rate time-driven cyclic executive, iff such a sequence exists.

Our OOA algorithm populates the sequence task[] from the last to the first element. It exploits the property that once a task is schedulable at a particular position in the sequence, it remains schedulable when the remaining tasks are placed at earlier positions.

Our OOA algorithm (see Algorithm 1) uses an auxiliary set of tasks T S,U that have not been put in the sequence task[] yet. The set T S,U is initialized to T S at line 1. Line 2 introduces a constant T S,min for the lower bound on the cycle time T S . Next, the algorithm populates the sequence task[] from the last to the first element (lines 3-15). At each iteration, it searches for a schedulable task from T S,U (lines 4-11). When a schedulable task is found, its index is put at the proper place in the sequence (line 7), the task is removed from T S,U (line 8), and a next iteration is started. When no schedulable task is found (line 13), the algorithm returns unschedulable. When at each iteration a schedulable task is found, the algorithm returns schedulable (line 16) and a schedulable sequence task[].

div.head: D. Proof sketch
div.p: The proof sketch consists of three steps. The first step maps the problem onto the classical problem of an optimal fixed-priority assignment of tasks on a single processor, in this case fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling of a set of tasks with a synchronous release where all tasks have the same (fixed) inter-arrival time [9]. The second step shows that the problem satisfies the conditions for applicability of Audsley's OPA (Optimal Priority Assignment) Algorithm [10]- [12]. The third step shows the similarity of our OOA and the OPA algorithm. Similar to the OPA algorithm, our OOA algorithm has a complexity O(n 2 ).

div.head: V. DISCUSSION
div.p: In the previous section, we presented two task orders for system S I that are both schedulable under a single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executive, i.e. {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 } in Section IV-B and {τ 3 , τ 2 , τ 1 } using our OOA-algorithm in Section IV-C. Although both task orders are schedulable, the former is preferred given the larger value for the cycle time T SI it can achieve, i.e. 16 versus 15.
The advantage of a larger cycle time T S follows from the following lemma [8].
Lemma 2. Whenever a system S is schedulable under a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive with a cycle time of T S , a fraction f S,gain (T S ) given by
div.formula: T S - 1≤i≤n WC i T S ≤ f S,gain (T S ) ≤ T S - 1≤i≤n BC i
div.p: T S of the time can be gained for background processing by a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive compared to a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive.

For system S I , we find for a task order • {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 } and T SI = 16: 1 16 ≤ f SI,gain (16) ≤ 5 16 ; • {τ 3 , τ 2 , τ 1 } and T SI = 15: 0 15 ≤ f SI,gain (15) ≤ 4 15 . Hence, a task order {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 } guarantees more spare time to reduce energy consumption or improve average response time of firm and soft tasks executed in the background.
Enhancing our OOA algorithm such that it determines an order with a maximum achievable T S is a topic of future work.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presented a conjecture for an optimal order assignment (OOA) algorithm for a system S and a task set T S , scheduled using a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. We merely presented a sketch of a proof of the conjecture. We illustrated our OOA algorithm by means of an example system. The algorithm does not necessarily yield an order with a maximum achievable T S , however. Enhancing our OOA-algorithm in such a way that it returns a schedulable task order with a maximum achievable T S , whenever a schedulable task order exists, is a topic of future work.
